subject: research/challenge-window
professional: a senior mechanism-design / blockchain-economics researcher who reviews fraud-proof and censorship-resistance papers (the AFT / FC programme-committee reader). First checks: is the attacker's dynamic programme right and optimal over all policies, are the headline windows reproducible, and what does this add over Berger, Felten, Mamageishvili and Sudakov, 'Economic Censorship Games in Fraud Proofs' (arXiv 2502.20334, 2025), which models the same bribe-the-proposer censorship of a challenge window

evidence.correctness: Ran the 9 tests (OK, 0.08 s) and run.py in a scratch copy: results.txt regenerates byte-for-byte, figure.py regenerates window_vs_stake.svg identically. Independent recomputation (scratchpad chk/recompute.py): (1) exact-Fraction enumeration of every per-block bribe policy over all 2^w owner patterns, 60 random instances w<=7, max |diff| vs value() = 2.6e-14, so the recursion is the true optimum; (2) E2 means by hand from the binomial (attacker always bribes since b<=S): 46.5, 33.0, 19.5, 6.0, matching V; (3) E3 63 = ceil(100/1.6), luck 2 and 1; (4) E4 windows 25,10,5,3,2,1 = ceil(100/(0.4 S)); (5) E6 w=4 -17.6 and -28.0 by hand; (6) E7 25.0 and 12.5 = 100/(0.4*10), 100/(0.8*10). Every number reproduces. Deductions: window_closed and window_luck raise ZeroDivisionError at rho=0 (no attacker proposers, a valid case; true window for G=100,S=50,b=80 is 2), and the MC agreement is 2.5 s.e. at w=6, not within 1.5 as claimed (a statistical fluctuation, not a bug).
evidence.completeness: README and whitepaper promise E1-E7, the closed form, the pure limits, the stake inversion and a figure; all exist and regenerate. The README test count (9) and runtime (<1 s) are right. No stubs or TODOs. research/_audit/audit.json lists the project as outcome not-run. The live page could not be loaded (proxy 000), so it is not scored.
evidence.verification: PYTHONPATH=src python3.13 -m unittest discover -s tests: 9 tests OK. The closed form is checked against the DP on 1,500 random instances, and MC against V. Five seeded mutants via quality_mutate.py: only the bribe-window formula was caught (1 of 5). Survived: dropping the bribe cost from the caught payoff in simulate_policy (the MC test uses b<=S so the attacker is never caught); dropping (1-rho) from the prefix-plan cost (the test only checks adaptive >= prefix); shifting the bribe/gamble threshold by 1 (wrong on 4 of 100,000 instances, so 1,500 random draws miss it); and cutting the stake bisection from 200 to 12 steps.
evidence.craft: Read model.py (100 lines), run.py, figure.py and test_model.py. The code is small, clean stdlib with docstrings. figure.py parses results.txt rather than retyping. Defects: no input guards (rho in {0,1}, b=0 all raise bare ZeroDivisionError or hit the cap); the window_luck docstring is garbled ('b = infinity is impossible; b -> 0 is the opposite'); unused `import math` in run.py and tests; one test line asserts the luck bound and then a weaker min() bound that it already implies.
evidence.claims: Checked against results.txt: 0/5000 mismatches (pass), 100-170x (106-167, pass), 63 blocks for S=10..1600 (pass), S*w = 250 for S=10-50 (pass), E7 25.0/12.5/inf (pass), 9 tests (pass). Fails: 'Monte Carlo within 1.5 s.e.' (w=3 is 1.7 and w=6 is 2.5 s.e.); 'the exact window is never below the smaller of the two' understates what holds (it is never below the larger, 0 of 20,000 instances, because bribe-every-block and never-bribe are both feasible policies); 'the adaptive structure changes the attacker's expected loss, not the window' is wrong as a takeaway: in 1,076 of 20,000 random instances the adaptive window is longer than the prefix plan's (G=100,S=5,rho=.9,b=40: 36 vs 29), and those are exactly the cases where it exceeds both pure limits. The contributions list claims the recursion and the fee-funded law as new with no reference to the prior work.
evidence.fitness: The nearest prior work is Berger, Felten, Mamageishvili and Sudakov 2025 (arXiv 2502.20334, Offchain Labs), which models bribing proposers to censor a fraud-proof challenge over a window, with the defender raising inclusion tips, and sizes the defender budget. Earlier: Winzer, Herd and Faust 2019 (temporary censorship attacks with rational miners), Tsabary et al. 2021 (MAD-HTLC, bribing miners to censor before a timeout), and Fox, Pai and Resnick 2023 (censorship cost = outbidding the fee in every block). None is cited; the whitepaper has no references at all. Given those, results (ii) and (iii) are one-line consequences of the bribe-every-block bound (attacker pays (1-rho) b per block, so w = G/((1-rho)b), and b = theta S gives the 1/S law), and (i) is driven by the chosen b=1 against G=100. The model is a one-player DP with exogenous constant b and rho, which is the case Berger et al. go beyond (the defender responds with tips). The one non-trivial result the code contains, that for b > S the gamble-then-bribe attacker pushes the window above both pure limits, is not stated. A researcher could not build on this as a contribution without repositioning it; a 23-line whitepaper is far from the research brief's PhD-level programme bar.
evidence.domain: The recursion and its solution are standard optimal stopping/control and are right. A practitioner would object to: constant exogenous bribe price with no competition from the challenger's own fee (only partly addressed by b = theta S), ignoring that real windows are days of blocks set for liveness and social coordination (Optimism and Arbitrum 7 days), no treatment of proposer collusion or PBS/builder markets, and the assumption of an always-present challenger. Section 4 states several of these limits honestly.

defects.what: No prior work cited; the whitepaper has zero references. Berger, Felten, Mamageishvili and Sudakov 2025 (arXiv 2502.20334) model the same bribe-proposers-to-censor-a-fraud-proof-challenge problem with a responding defender; Winzer et al. 2019, MAD-HTLC 2021 and Fox-Pai-Resnick 2023 give the per-block censorship cost. Results (ii) and (iii) are listed as contributions though they follow in one line from the bribe-every-block bound

'the adaptive structure changes the attacker's expected loss, not the window' is a wrong takeaway: the adaptive window exceeds the prefix plan's (and both pure limits) in 1,076 of 20,000 random instances, by up to ~25% (G=100,S=5,rho=.9,b=40: 36 vs 29). The paper's only non-trivial result is unstated, and the stated bound 'never below the smaller of the two' should be 'never below the larger'
Abstract says MC matches 'within 1.5 s.e.'; its own results.txt shows 1.7 and 2.5 s.e. at w=3 and w=6

Tests leave most core logic unpinned: 4 of 5 seeded mutants survive (caught-payoff bribe cost in simulate_policy, prefix-plan cost, bribe/gamble threshold off by one, bisection depth). The MC test uses b<=S so the caught branch never runs
window_closed and window_luck raise ZeroDivisionError at rho=0 (no attacker-owned proposers, a valid case) and window_luck at rho=1; no input validation
Model takes b and rho as exogenous constants with no defender response, the case the prior work goes beyond; real challenge windows (7 days) are not related to the model's block counts
Garbled window_luck docstring, unused imports in run.py and tests, redundant min() assertion

verdict: Below the bar. The arithmetic is right: an exact policy enumeration, the binomial means and hand calculations of E3, E4, E6 and E7 all reproduce, and run.py and the figure regenerate byte-for-byte. Claims (2) and verification (2) fail the gate. The paper says the adaptive attacker changes loss and not the window, but 5% of random instances show a longer window. It also misstates its MC agreement, and 4 of 5 seeded mutants survive. On novelty it cites nothing, although Berger, Felten, Mamageishvili and Sudakov (2025) treat the same censorship-of-challenge problem, and its stake results are one-line corollaries of the bribe-every-block bound. Fitness 1: a short stylised note, not a PhD-level contribution.
